conventions.convention: An operator is a forward map and need not be linear. Admissible truth/operator pairs form a specified subset of the product, not necessarily the full product.
Additive observations use a specified data sigma-algebra and measurable translations. Noise laws are probability measures on that measurable space.

Operator mismatch, noise-law mismatch, statistical-model misspecification, and prior-support mismatch are distinct. Prior-support mismatch means that a positive-radius open ball around the specified true index has prior mass zero.

The lower bound uses one common randomized decision kernel under both specifications, measurable metric-loss sections, equal sampling laws, and extended nonnegative risks. Deterministic measurable rules are included.
The positive-modulus example treats the restricted configuration set as its parameter class, with the restricted sum metric and target equal to the truth coordinate.
The identical-law example equips both real data and real actions with power-set sigma-algebras; its noise law is any probability measure on that space, with a Dirac measure explicitly available.

load_bearing.statement: A specified set C contained in U × A records admissible truth/operator pairs. Measurable translations of a probability noise law define sampling laws. Operator mismatch, noise-law mismatch, model misspecification, and prior-support mismatch are distinct properties.

For two admissible specifications with targets q₀ and q₁ in a metric target space, measurable metric-loss sections, and one randomized decision rule used under both specifications, if P₀ = P₁ and Δ = d_Q(q₀,q₁), then max{R₀(δ), R₁(δ)} ≥ Δ/2.

concerns.concern: Fact F9 says that the constant function on Q has integral “Δμ(𝖸)=Δ” under a probability measure μ. For its inner-integral application μ = δ(y,·) is a measure on Q, so μ(𝖸) is generally undefined; the expression should use the underlying integration space. The intended constant-integral identity is elementary and the lower bound remains valid.
